Tophet
TOH-fet
n. proper (biblical place; cultic site in the Valley of Hinnom)
Hebrew tōpheth (Tophet, Topheth; etymology disputed; possibly from a root meaning “fire-place” or “spitting,” but most commonly derived from an Aramaic root tāph, drum, because drummers may have beaten drums to drown the cries of sacrificed children; some scholars propose deliberate vocalization with the vowels of bōsheth, shame, as a polemical alteration of the site's original name). The site is consistently located in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom; later Gehenna), south and southwest of Jerusalem.

Biblical Definition

Tophet was a cultic installation in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) outside Jerusalem where children were burned as offerings to the god Molech — the most extreme expression of Canaanite idolatry that Israel repeatedly fell into during the period of the kings. Jeremiah 7:31 names the site precisely: “They have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire — which I did not command, and which never came into My heart.” The divine response is visceral: this was not a worship God tolerated, accommodated, or permitted in any modified form; it was a command that “never came into My heart.” Jeremiah 19:6 announces the doom that will rename the site: “the days are coming...that this place shall no more be called Tophet or the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.” The reforming king Josiah defiled Topheth deliberately so that it could no longer be used for child sacrifice: “And he defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.” (2 Kgs 23:10). Isaiah 30:33 uses the prepared “Tophet” as an image of divine judgment: “For Tophet was established of old, yes, for the king it is prepared.” The Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) became in Jewish thought the paradigmatic image of divine judgment — what the New Testament names Gehenna, the lake of fire, the place of eternal conscious punishment for the unredeemed. Tophet is thus a prophetic hinge: the place where Israel desecrated the image of God in children becomes the prototype of the place where God vindicates that desecration with final, unquenchable judgment.

Webster 1828 Definition

A cultic site in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem where Israelites burned children in fire to Molech, condemned as abomination by Jeremiah and defiled by Josiah; the Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) became the New Testament Gehenna — the prototype of eternal judgment — in part because of Tophet's history of desecrated image-bearers.

TOPHET, n. (Heb. tōpheth; also Topheth). A cultic installation or “high place” in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom), south-southwest of Jerusalem, where children were burned as sacrificial offerings to Molech. Mentioned in Jeremiah 7:31, 19:6, 11, 14; 2 Kings 23:10; and Isaiah 30:33.

The rite performed at Tophet was the most extreme apostasy the kings of Judah committed: Ahaz “his children in the fire” (2 Chr 28:3); Manasseh “made his children pass through the fire” (2 Chr 33:6); common Israelites followed suit at the Tophet installation. These were not superstitious accidents; they were deliberate acts of child sacrifice to a false god, undertaken while maintaining the temple cult in Jerusalem.

Jeremiah's prophecy against Tophet (Jer 7:31–34; 19:1–15) is among the most direct prophetic condemnations in the Hebrew prophets. The Valley of Hinnom — Ge-Hinnom — would become the Valley of Slaughter. No longer would it be a cult site; it would become a burial ground too full to bury more. The inversion of the child-sacrifice site into a mass grave anticipates the New Testament use of Ge-Hinnom as the name for eschatological judgment.

Josiah's defilement of Tophet (2 Kgs 23:10) was part of his comprehensive reform under the recovered Law (2 Kgs 22–23); he rendered the site ritually unclean so that child sacrifice could not resume. The reform did not outlast him; the prophets condemn the practice as continuing after his death.

The connection to Gehenna (New Testament) is geographical and theological: the same valley where children were burned to Molech becomes, in Jewish intertestamental tradition and then in Jesus' teaching (Matt 5:22, 29; Mark 9:43–48; Luke 12:5), the prototype of the unquenchable fire of divine judgment — the righteous counterpoint to the desecration that occurred there.

Key Scripture

Jeremiah 7:31 — "And they have built the high places of Tophet, which is in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire — which I did not command, and which never came into My heart."

2 Kings 23:10 — "And he defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech."

Jeremiah 19:6 — "Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that this place shall no more be called Tophet, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of slaughter."

Isaiah 30:33 — "For Tophet is ordained of old; yea, for the king it is prepared; he hath made it deep and large: the pile thereof is fire and much wood; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it."

Modern Corruption

Modern critical scholarship often contextualizes Tophet within comparative Canaanite religion in ways that minimize the biblical text's moral horror; some archaeologists have disputed whether child sacrifice actually occurred, interpreting the site as a burial ground for stillborn infants — a reading the prophetic texts do not support.

expand to see more

The “tophet hypothesis” in modern Phoenician archaeology — associated with Lawrence Stager and others — interprets ancient Near Eastern tophets as infant burial grounds for children who died naturally, not as sites of child sacrifice. Some scholars have applied this hypothesis to the Jerusalem Tophet, suggesting Jeremiah's condemnation was misidentifying burial customs as sacrifice. But the biblical text is explicit: the prophets condemn burning children in fire as an offering to Molech; the vocabulary is sacrificial, not funerary. “Pass through the fire” is the standard biblical idiom for child sacrifice. Archaeologically-driven reinterpretation that contradicts the prophetic testimony is historical-critical assumption operating against the text's plain meaning.

Liberal progressive readings have used Tophet's history to construct arguments against the God of the Old Testament as complicit in ancient violence — the so-called “dark passages” critique. The biblical text itself forecloses this: Jeremiah 7:31 explicitly states that Tophet's rites were something God “did not command and never came into My heart.” The atrocity was Israel's apostasy, not divine sanction. The same God who condemns Tophet is the God who will judge it — as Isaiah 30:33 makes plain in its use of Tophet as a prophetic image of divine wrath against the enemies of His people.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) in the Kidron-Hinnom valley system south of Jerusalem; associated with the cult of Molech condemned throughout the Mosaic legislation; prophetically renamed as the site of divine judgment; became the geographical root of the New Testament Gehenna.

expand to see more

Valley of the Son of Hinnom (Ge Ben-Hinnom) — the full Hebrew name of the valley in which Tophet was located; south and southwest of Jerusalem, below the walls of the old city; identified with Gehenna in New Testament usage (transliteration of Ge-Hinnom into Greek as Geenna).

Molech (Molek) — the deity to whom children were burned at Tophet; Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2–5 explicitly prohibit giving children to Molech; the practice is the most extreme form of the idolatry the Mosaic covenant forbids — the desecration of image-bearers as offerings to a false god.

Ahaz and Manasseh — the two kings of Judah most explicitly linked to Tophet practices (2 Chr 28:3; 33:6); their reigns represent the low ebb of the Davidic monarchy and the deepest penetration of Canaanite abominations into the covenant people.

Josiah's reform (2 Kgs 23:10) — part of the comprehensive covenant renewal after the Law was found in the temple; Josiah's deliberate defilement of Tophet was an act of prophylactic judgment against the site itself, rendering it ritually unclean for cultic use.

Gehenna in the New Testament — Jesus uses Ge-Hinnom (Geenna) as the standard word for the eternal conscious punishment of the wicked (Matt 5:22, 29, 30; 10:28; 23:33; Mark 9:43–48); the choice of this geography is theologically loaded: the place of desecrated image-bearers becomes the image of the place where the desecrators themselves face God's unquenchable judgment.

Usage

"The history of Tophet is a warning against the drift of a people who know God's law into the practices of surrounding nations; Israel did not arrive at Tophet in a single apostasy but through generations of tolerated compromise with Canaanite religion."

"Jeremiah's declaration that Tophet's practices “never came into My heart” is a direct refutation of any theology that reads the God of the Old Testament as sanctioning violence against the vulnerable; the prophetic tradition speaks with one voice on Tophet: it is abomination."

"The connection between Tophet and Gehenna teaches a biblical anthropology: every human life is an image-bearer whose destruction for utilitarian or cultic ends is an assault on the God whose image is borne; the judgment that befalls the desecrators at Ge-Hinnom is proportionate to the honor God places on the image-bearers they destroyed."
